questions.stem: According to the James-Lange theory, an emotion is:
options: general arousal that is labelled using cues from the situation
a learnt habit that is strengthened by rewards from other people
the experience of the bodily changes that a situation produces
a judgement about a situation that happens before any arousal at all
questions.explanation: William James and Carl Lange proposed that a stimulus first triggers bodily changes, such as a racing heart, and that the emotion is our perception of those changes. Labelling general arousal using situational cues is the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory.

questions.stem: Walking home at night, Ava hears footsteps behind her. Her heart pounds and she starts to tremble. According to the James-Lange theory, she feels afraid because:
options: her thalamus sends signals to her cortex first
she copies the fear shown by other people nearby
she notices her body pounding and trembling
she decides the footsteps are a threat to her
questions.explanation: James-Lange reverses the common-sense order: Ava does not tremble because she is afraid; she is afraid because she perceives herself trembling. A decision that the footsteps are a threat would come first in an appraisal account.

questions.stem: Walter Cannon criticised the James-Lange theory. Which point was part of his argument?
options: Very similar bodily changes occur in different emotions, so they cannot tell emotions apart
Bodily changes happen much faster than emotions, so they must come after the emotion is felt
Emotions occur only in humans, so research on animals cannot tell us anything about them
Cognitive labels are unnecessary, because each emotion has its own unique pattern of arousal
questions.explanation: Cannon argued that arousal such as a racing heart is much the same in fear, anger and excitement, so it cannot by itself produce distinct emotions, and that internal organs respond too slowly. He proposed that the thalamus triggers the bodily response and the felt emotion at the same time.

questions.stem: The Cannon-Bard theory proposes that, when we meet an emotional stimulus:
options: the facial expression comes first and then produces the matching emotion
the thalamus triggers bodily arousal and the felt emotion at the same time
bodily arousal comes first, and the emotion is the perception of that arousal
general arousal is labelled as an emotion using cues found in the situation
questions.explanation: Cannon and Bard argued that the thalamus sends signals at the same time to the cortex, producing the felt emotion, and to the body, producing arousal; neither causes the other. Arousal first, then emotion, is the James-Lange theory.

questions.stem: The Schachter-Singer two-factor theory states that emotion depends on:
options: physiological arousal plus a cognitive label for it
physiological arousal alone, without any thinking
the activity of the thalamus without any arousal
facial expressions alone, without any arousal at all
questions.explanation: Schachter and Singer proposed that we experience general arousal and then use cues in the situation to label it as a particular emotion; both factors are needed. Arousal alone was the James-Lange position.

questions.stem: In Schachter and Singer's (1962) study, participants injected with adrenaline were told it was a vitamin. Some were not told about its real effects. Why did those uninformed participants matter most to the theory?
options: They had arousal they could not explain, so they looked to their surroundings for a label
They had no arousal at all, so any emotion they reported must have come from the vitamin itself
They knew exactly what to expect, so they ignored the behaviour of the confederate
They were told the true purpose, so their answers could not be affected by deception
questions.explanation: Participants without an explanation for their racing heart were expected to label it using cues, such as a euphoric or angry confederate, and this is what the theory predicted. Informed participants could attribute their arousal to the injection.

questions.stem: Which ethical concern is most clearly raised by Schachter and Singer's procedure?
options: Participants were told the true aim of the study, which made the results invalid
Participants were deceived about the injection and given a drug without full informed consent
Participants were paid far too much, which meant they felt forced to stay until the very end
Participants were all tested together in large groups, which breached confidentiality
questions.explanation: Participants were misled about what they were injected with and the purpose of the study, so their consent was not fully informed, and adrenaline can cause discomfort. Today such deception would need strong justification, ethics approval and a thorough debrief.

questions.stem: After running up the stairs, Leo's heart is still racing when a friend jokes about him. He snaps angrily. Which theory best explains why his anger was stronger than usual?
options: Cannon's theory, because arousal and emotion are always completely unrelated
Two-factor theory, because exercise produces a pattern of arousal unique to anger
Two-factor theory, because leftover arousal from exercise was labelled as anger
James-Lange theory, because his heart rate came from his anger rather than running
questions.explanation: Arousal from the stairs carried over, and the situation (the joke) led Leo to label it as anger, so his anger was intensified. This kind of misattribution of arousal is predicted by the two-factor theory.

questions.stem: In 'The Neuroscience of Emotion' (2018), Ralph Adolphs and David Anderson argue that emotions should be studied as:
options: conscious feelings that can only ever be studied by asking people to describe them
learnt habits that have no basis in the brain or in the body at all
cultural labels that differ completely from one society to the next one
internal brain states with functions, which can be investigated in animals too
questions.explanation: Adolphs and Anderson treat emotions as functional internal states produced by the brain, separate from conscious feelings, so they can be studied with neuroscience methods across species. This contrasts with relying only on people's reports of how they feel.

questions.stem: S.M. is a woman with damage to the amygdala on both sides of her brain. Studies found she had particular difficulty recognising which emotion in other people's faces?
options: Happiness
Surprise
Disgust
Fear
questions.explanation: Adolphs and colleagues (1994) found S.M. was especially impaired at recognising fear in facial expressions, and she also shows unusually little fear herself. This supports the amygdala's role in fear processing.

questions.stem: Why do case studies of brain damage, such as S.M., add to what fMRI studies of healthy people can show about emotion?
options: fMRI cannot record brain activity at all while participants view emotional faces
Case studies can be repeated easily with many people who have the same damage
Damage shows whether an area is needed for a function, not just active during it
Case studies use large random samples, so they generalise better than fMRI
questions.explanation: fMRI shows which areas are associated with a task; if losing an area removes a function, that suggests the area is necessary for it. Case studies have their own limits: they involve one person and cannot be repeated or easily generalised.

questions.stem: Which brain structure is most closely linked to detecting threats and producing fear responses?
options: Amygdala
Cerebellum
Occipital lobe
Medulla
questions.explanation: The amygdala, part of the limbic system, rapidly evaluates the emotional significance of stimuli, especially threats, and triggers fear responses. The cerebellum coordinates movement and the occipital lobe processes vision.

questions.stem: Which list gives the six basic emotions that Paul Ekman proposed are expressed in the same way across cultures?
options: Happiness, sadness, anger, fear, shame, jealousy
Happiness, guilt, anger, pride, surprise, disgust
Love, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, boredom
Happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust
questions.explanation: Ekman proposed six basic emotions with universal facial expressions: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise and disgust. Emotions such as shame, guilt and pride were seen as more dependent on culture.

questions.stem: Why did Ekman and Friesen (1971) study the Fore people of Papua New Guinea?
options: They lived in a large city, so it was easy to recruit a large random sample of participants
They had been raised watching Western films, so they could recognise every expression shown to them
They spoke English as a first language, so the stories could be given without translation
They had little exposure to Western media, so they could not have learnt Western expressions from it
questions.explanation: If people with little contact with Western media could match faces to emotional stories, the expressions were unlikely to be learnt from that media, supporting universality. The Fore matched most expressions well, though some confused fear with surprise.

questions.stem: Japanese and American students watched stressful films. Alone, both groups showed similar expressions of disgust and fear. With an experimenter present, Japanese students more often smiled. Ekman explained this with:
options: basic emotions, which are expressed differently in every culture
the James-Lange theory, because their arousal changed when in company
facial feedback, because smiling had made the films less stressful
display rules, the cultural norms for when and how emotions are shown
questions.explanation: The similar expressions when alone suggested a universal response, while the masking in company reflected display rules, learnt cultural norms about showing emotion in front of others. Basic emotions are proposed to be universal, not culture-specific.

questions.stem: Ekman and Friesen developed the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). What does it allow researchers to do?
options: Measure heart rate and sweating to find out exactly which emotion a person feels
Read a person's thoughts from the activity of their facial nerves
Diagnose mental disorders from a single photograph of a person's face
Code facial expressions objectively from the movements of individual muscles
questions.explanation: FACS breaks expressions into action units based on facial muscle movements, making the coding of expressions more objective and reliable between raters. It describes visible movements; it does not read thoughts or diagnose disorders.

questions.stem: Some critics argue that Ekman's evidence for universal expressions was inflated by the method of asking people to choose from a short list of emotion words. Why might this matter?
options: A forced choice can produce agreement that would not appear if people named emotions freely
Lists of words always reduce agreement between cultures, which hides a universal pattern
Choosing from a list removes the need for any translation between languages
The method measured heart rate rather than recognition of facial expressions
questions.explanation: When people must pick from a few labels, they can reach the 'right' answer by elimination, so agreement may be higher than in free labelling. This criticism questions how strong the evidence for universality is, not whether expressions vary at all.

questions.stem: Kleinke, Peterson and Rutledge (1998) asked participants to make happy or sad facial expressions. What did they find?
options: Negative expressions raised mood, because participants found the task amusing
Mood changed only when participants were shown other people's faces as well
Positive expressions raised mood and negative ones lowered it, more so with a mirror
Facial expressions had no effect on mood unless participants were told the study's aim
questions.explanation: Making a positive expression increased reported positive mood and making a negative one decreased it, and watching oneself in a mirror strengthened the effect. This supports the facial feedback hypothesis that expressions can influence emotion.

questions.stem: Strack and colleagues (1988) reported that holding a pen in the teeth (producing a smile) made cartoons seem funnier. In 2016, seventeen labs repeated the study. What did this show?
options: The original authors had used too many participants, so the effect disappeared
The original effect was not replicated, so the claim is weaker than once believed
The original effect was much larger than first reported, so the claim is now proven
The study could not be repeated, because no one could find any cartoons to use
questions.explanation: The large registered replication found no reliable effect of pen position on cartoon ratings. Replication is how science checks findings; this result weakened the strong version of the facial feedback claim, although debate continues.

questions.stem: Williams and Bargh (2008) reported that people briefly holding a hot coffee judged a stranger as having a 'warmer' personality than those holding iced coffee. How should a student treat this finding today?
options: With caution, because larger later studies failed to find the effect
As settled, because it was published in a well-known scientific journal
As proof that warm drinks improve everyone's mood for the whole day
As invalid, because coffee cannot be used in psychology experiments
questions.explanation: Larger, more careful replications found little or no effect, so the original result may have been a false positive from a small sample. Publication in a major journal does not guarantee a finding is reliable, and the study measured judgements of others, not general mood.

questions.stem: Salovey and Mayer (1990) defined emotional intelligence as the ability to:
options: remember emotional events in more detail than neutral ones
hide all emotions so that others cannot tell how one feels
perceive, understand and manage one's own and others' emotions
solve abstract problems quickly without being affected by emotion
questions.explanation: Emotional intelligence describes abilities to recognise emotions in oneself and others, use emotions in thinking, understand them and manage them. Hiding all emotions is not emotional intelligence; managing emotions means regulating them appropriately.

questions.stem: Which list gives the four branches of Mayer and Salovey's ability model of emotional intelligence?
options: Perceiving, using, understanding and managing emotions
Openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness and stability
Preconventional, conventional, postconventional and universal
Arousal, appraisal, labelling and expressing emotions
questions.explanation: The ability model's four branches are perceiving emotions, using emotions to help thinking, understanding emotions and managing emotions. The second list contains Big Five traits, and the third mixes up Kohlberg's levels.

questions.stem: Daniel Goleman's popular 1995 book claimed emotional intelligence could matter more than IQ, and many workplaces now run 'EQ' training. Which is the strongest scientific concern?
options: EQ training is illegal in most workplaces, so its results cannot be studied
Emotions have no effect on behaviour at work, so the concept is meaningless
Many EQ measures overlap heavily with personality traits and some claims outran the evidence
Emotional intelligence has been shown to be identical to IQ in every single study of it
questions.explanation: Self-report EQ scales correlate strongly with personality traits such as agreeableness and low neuroticism, raising questions about whether they measure anything new, and claims that EQ outweighs IQ went beyond the research. This shows how a concept can spread through workplaces ahead of the evidence.

questions.stem: A school introduces a social and emotional learning program and reports that students 'feel happier'. What would give the strongest evidence that the program works?
options: Comparing similar students in schools with and without the program on measured outcomes
Asking the teachers who designed the program whether they personally think it has worked well
Counting how many lessons in the program were delivered over the school year
Publishing positive comments from a few students in the school newsletter
questions.explanation: A comparison group allows researchers to tell whether changes are due to the program rather than other factors, such as students growing older. The designers' opinions and selected comments are open to bias.

questions.stem: In Kohlberg's theory, moral development progresses through which three levels, in order?
options: Preconventional, conventional, postconventional
Conventional, preconventional, postconventional
Postconventional, conventional, preconventional
Sensorimotor, concrete operational, formal operational
questions.explanation: Kohlberg proposed three levels, each with two stages: preconventional (avoiding punishment, self-interest), conventional (approval and law and order) and postconventional (social contract and universal principles). The last list is Piaget's cognitive stages.

questions.stem: In Kohlberg's research, people responded to dilemmas such as whether Heinz should steal a drug to save his dying wife. How was a person's stage decided?
options: From how strongly their heart rate rose while thinking about it
From the reasoning they gave, not from whether they said yes or no
From whether they said that Heinz should steal the drug or should not
From how quickly they gave an answer to each of the dilemmas
questions.explanation: Kohlberg was interested in the structure of moral reasoning; two people could give the same answer for reasons at very different stages. Speed of response and physiological arousal were not part of his scoring.

questions.stem: Asked why he does not cheat on tests, a nine-year-old says, 'Because I'd get caught and get a detention.' This reasoning fits which of Kohlberg's levels?
options: Preconventional
Conventional
Postconventional
Universal
questions.explanation: Reasoning based on avoiding punishment is stage 1, at the preconventional level. Conventional reasoning focuses on approval from others or upholding laws and rules, and postconventional reasoning on rights and principles.

questions.stem: Priya argues, 'The law against stealing exists to protect people's lives, so when a law fails to protect a life, saving the life matters more.' This fits which of Kohlberg's levels?
options: Conventional, because she wants to keep the approval of other people
Preconventional, because she is focused on avoiding being punished
Conventional, because she believes laws must be obeyed in every case
Postconventional, because laws are judged against rights and principles
questions.explanation: Priya treats laws as tools that serve deeper values and can be overridden when they fail to protect basic rights, which is postconventional reasoning. Conventional reasoning would emphasise obeying the law to maintain social order.

questions.stem: Asked why she helps her neighbours, Grace says, 'Because good people help others, and I want everyone to see me as a good person.' This reasoning fits which of Kohlberg's levels?
options: Preconventional, because it seeks a direct reward in exchange for the help
Conventional, because it seeks approval by meeting others' expectations
Preconventional, because it seeks to avoid a punishment from adults
Postconventional, because it applies self-chosen universal principles
questions.explanation: Wanting to be seen as a good person by living up to others' expectations is stage 3, at the conventional level. Postconventional reasoning would rest on principles a person holds whatever others think.

questions.stem: A student says, 'I should obey road rules because society would fall apart if everyone ignored the law.' This is an example of:
options: conventional reasoning focused on maintaining social order
preconventional reasoning focused on getting a reward
postconventional reasoning focused on universal principles
preconventional reasoning focused on avoiding punishment
questions.explanation: Upholding laws to maintain social order is stage 4, the 'law and order' stage of the conventional level. Postconventional reasoning would ask whether a law serves rights and principles, not just whether it keeps order.

questions.stem: Carol Gilligan (1982) criticised Kohlberg's theory mainly because:
options: it found that women always reach higher stages of moral reasoning than do men of the same age
it relied only on brain imaging rather than on interviews about dilemmas with participants
it argued that moral reasoning has no connection to cognitive development of any kind
it was built from male participants and undervalued reasoning based on care and relationships
questions.explanation: Kohlberg's original research followed boys, and Gilligan argued his scoring favoured a justice orientation and ranked an ethic of care lower, which could make women appear less morally developed. She proposed care as an equally valid moral orientation.

questions.stem: Researchers have found that people in some collectivist cultures rarely reach Kohlberg's postconventional stages. Which interpretation reflects a valid criticism of the theory?
options: Moral reasoning cannot be studied in other cultures because dilemmas cannot be translated
Kohlberg's stages are proven to apply identically in every culture that has been studied
The stages may reflect Western values about individual rights rather than a universal sequence
People in collectivist cultures must have less developed brains than those in other cultures
questions.explanation: Postconventional reasoning emphasises individual rights and abstract principles, which are more valued in Western, individualist cultures. Reasoning centred on family and community may be mature in its own context, so the theory may be culturally biased.

questions.stem: A student practises the guitar every night simply because she enjoys it. Her motivation is:
options: extrinsic
vicarious
conditioned
intrinsic
questions.explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from the enjoyment or interest of the activity itself. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards or pressures, such as marks, money or praise.

questions.stem: A psychotherapist tells a client that dreaming of falling 'reveals a hidden fear of losing control'. Why do many psychologists regard this kind of dream analysis as scientifically weak?
options: Brain imaging has shown that dreams are identical in every person every night
Dream analysis has been tested in large trials and found to be fully proven
Interpretations cannot be tested, because any dream can be read to fit the theory
Dreams occur only during the day, so they cannot be recorded in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Dream analysis comes from the psychoanalytic perspective; because the meaning of a dream is decided by the interpreter, there is no result that could show an interpretation to be wrong. Claims that cannot be falsified cannot be tested scientifically.

questions.stem: A Year 11 student wants to replicate a facial expression and mood study with classmates. Which design is most appropriate for school students?
options: Tell volunteers the study is about memory and never explain its real purpose to them
Record classmates' facial expressions secretly during lessons without their knowledge
Ask volunteers to hold brief smiles or frowns, rate their mood, and debrief them afterwards
Show volunteers distressing images to make them sad before they hold any facial expression
questions.explanation: A brief, low-stakes task with informed consent, the right to withdraw and a debrief is appropriate for minors. Deliberately causing distress, undisclosed deception and secret recording would breach ethical guidelines for school research.

questions.stem: In a class study, students who held a smile rated their mood a mean of 6.8 out of 10, compared with 6.5 for those who held a neutral face. There were 10 students in each group. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: Smiling lowers mood, because the difference between the groups is so small
The results disprove the facial feedback hypothesis in every population
The difference is small and the samples tiny, so no firm conclusion can be drawn
Smiling clearly causes a large improvement in mood for every single student who was tested
questions.explanation: A 0.3-point difference with only 10 participants per group could easily be due to chance or individual differences, so the result neither supports nor disproves the hypothesis strongly. A larger sample and replication would be needed.

questions.stem: The facial feedback hypothesis proposes that:
options: emotions are always caused by the facial expressions of others
facial expressions are learnt only by watching Western media
faces show no emotion unless a person chooses to display it
facial expressions can influence the emotions a person feels
questions.explanation: The hypothesis holds that feedback from the facial muscles contributes to emotional experience, so smiling may make a person feel slightly happier. The evidence is mixed, with some well-known findings failing to replicate.
